paragraphs.heading: What cell division is
paragraphs.text: Cell division is how one parent cell becomes two daughter cells. It is usually one part of a bigger cell cycle, during which the cell first grows and copies its chromosomes, then splits. In every organism, each division comes after a single round of DNA replication. The central aim is to keep the original cell's genome intact: the genetic information in the chromosomes has to be copied, and the copy then shared out cleanly between the new cells.

paragraphs.heading: Two kinds in eukaryotes
paragraphs.text: Eukaryotes divide in two distinct ways. Mitosis is a vegetative division that keeps the chromosome number the same and gives daughter cells genetically identical to the parent. Meiosis makes haploid gametes for sexual reproduction, so a diploid parent with two chromosomes of each type gives daughters with just one of each. It runs through two divisions and ends with four haploid daughter cells. The first division separates homologous chromosomes, and the second separates the two sister chromatids that each already-copied chromosome carries.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: For a simple single-celled microorganism such as an amoeba, one division is reproduction: a whole new organism appears. Mitotic division can also make offspring of multicellular organisms, as when plants grow from cuttings. Sexually reproducing organisms start as a one-celled zygote, formed when two gametes fuse, and mitosis lets them develop from it. Once the adult is grown, mitosis keeps building and repairing the body. A human body goes through about 10 quadrillion cell divisions in a lifetime.

paragraphs.heading: Step by step in mitosis
paragraphs.text: Before dividing, a cell passes through interphase, which has three main phases: G₁, S and G₂. G₁ is a growth time that readies the cell for DNA replication, and the DNA is then copied during S. In mitosis, the division of the nucleus, the chromosomes, each made of two sister chromatids, typically line up on the metaphase plate before the chromatids split and go to the two daughter cells. Cytokinesis then divides the cytoplasm, organelles and cell membrane into two cells with roughly equal shares. Along the way, checkpoints detect and repair DNA damage, and they can halt the cycle by blocking certain cyclin-CDK complexes.

paragraphs.heading: How bacteria divide
paragraphs.text: Prokaryotes, meaning bacteria and archaea, usually divide by binary fission, sharing their genetic material equally between two daughter cells, though budding has also been seen. In bacteria, a protein complex called the divisome carries out division. It pinches in the inner and outer membranes and remodels the peptidoglycan cell wall at the site of the split. A tubulin-like protein called FtsZ is critical for building the contractile ring that does the dividing. Division in eukaryotes is more complicated than in these prokaryotes.
